name: Frequency Local Businesses
note: Finds independent local businesses that host or back community gatherings, and drafts one note each. Draft only.

offer.pitch: A free page and calendar for a local business and the gatherings it hosts, so regulars can find what is on.
offer.call_to_action: Put what you host where neighbors can see it

hunts.link_line: If you'd like a free page for your business on Frequency, start here:

playbook.seek: Who to find: independent local businesses in the region that already act like a community room: cafes and tea houses, bookstores, plant, record, game and craft shops, climbing and movement gyms, run, bike and surf shops, breweries and tasting rooms, farm stands and markets. Keep one only when a public page shows it hosts or backs something local: a run club, an open mic, a game night, a book club, a class, a pop-up market, or an events page or community board of its own.
playbook.signals: Strong signs, best first: an events or community page on its own site with something in the next 60 days; a named weekly or monthly gathering that meets there, such as a run club, a game night or an open mic; a club or group it sponsors by name; a community board, a workshop list or a "host your event here" line; an owner or manager named on the page. Weak signs: only sales and specials, or a single location of a chain.
playbook.where: Where to look: the business's own website and events page, city and chamber of commerce calendars, downtown and business association listings, and local news roundups of things to do.
playbook.queries: Searches that work: "<town> run club meets at", "<town> cafe open mic", "<town> bookstore book club", "<town> game store game night", "<town> brewery trivia community night", "<town> plant shop workshop", "<town> climbing gym community night", "<town> surf shop meetup", "<town> downtown association events". Use each area's own town names.
playbook.skip: Skip national chains and franchises, businesses with no sign of hosting anything, and anything that is only a sale, a happy hour or a promotion.
playbook.rank: Order leads.json best first, because only the first few are kept: an independent business with a named recurring gathering and a listed email comes first, then one with an events page and a contact form, then the rest. One lead per business, addressed to the owner or manager when the page names them.
playbook.record: In leads.json the event is the thing they host: event.title is its name or what kind of thing it is, event.url is the public page that shows it, and starts_at may be empty. The organizer is the business, with the owner's or manager's name when the page gives it.
playbook.note: Write a warm, human invite in four short paragraphs. 1: "Hi <first name>, <the thing they host, named loosely> at <their business> caught my eye, and I love what you are up to." You may add one short, true line about it and one emoji that fits them; never give a date, time, price or address, and never comment on how busy they are. 2: "I'm Daniel, a local community builder and the founder of Frequency!" 3: "Frequency is a free way for neighbors to find or start local, in-person Circles and events around what they love. Right now I'm focused on the local spots that give neighbors a reason to get together, and on making it easy for businesses like yours to bring more of them in." 4: one easy question that fits them, such as "Would you be interested in sharing your trivia night with neighbors nearby who are looking for something to do?", then "We're beta launching here in North County SD, and I would love for you to come check it out." Keep the quoted sentences as written. Use no exclamation mark besides the one in paragraph 2, and in a DM leave out the "Right now" sentence.
